extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of 19th-century American literary criticism and biography; scholars of oratory and poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging the public effectiveness, literary quality, and moral character of 19th-century American orators (e.g., Theodore Parker) and poets (e.g., John Greenleaf Whittier). Focuses on delivery, popular appeal, literary execution, moral force, and authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assimilation versus accumulation of learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning is not accumulation, but assimilation; every man's real acquirements must pass into his own organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mere hoarding of facts. Hasty or undue 'nutrition' (over-accumulation) can impair the quality of thought; a scholar should cultivate and internalize knowledge rather than exhaustively collect it. (Text: 'Learning is not accumulation, but assimilation; every man's real acquirements must pass into his own organization...undue or hasty nutrition does no good.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness and accuracy of scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: Thorough industry in compilation and research — patient investigation that yields reliable detail — is a strength, though occasional mistakes may occur amid multiplicity of details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value patient, exhaustive work (example: discovering an obscure vellum quarto). But recognize limits: wide-ranging industry can produce occasional errors; critics may note hasty conclusions when speed is extreme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to popularize complex thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to translate and present ideas so that tens of thousands understand what others (e.g., Emerson) told to hundreds; the popularizer's role is distinct from, but complementary to, the original thinker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess effectiveness by audience reach and comprehension: does the speaker/writer make abstruse ideas accessible without destroying their essence? ('he yet translated for tens of thousands that which Emerson spoke to hundreds only').

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to audience preferences (structure & statistics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness of and accommodation to audience tastes — e.g., New Englanders' liking for 'a philosophical arrangement and a plenty of statistics' — by systematically organizing material and supplying facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good public discourse often requires clear arrangement and supporting data. Parker deliberately provided both systematic structure and abundant statistics to suit his public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and lucidity of oral delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear, lucid, and composed elocution that grips audiences even with largely factual, unadorned content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delivery can compensate for lack of ornament: sustained composure, section-by-section presentation, and lucid pacing can make long factual lectures compelling ('Nearly two hours of almost unadorned fact...the lyceum audience listened to it as if an angel sang to them').

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational versatility and geniality
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity to converse on any subject with exhaustless information and without arrogance; ability to monopolize conversation by sheer charm rather than impatience with others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate social/colloquial effectiveness by breadth of knowledge, lack of conversational arrogance, and capacity to enchant varied company (examples: talking on agriculture, Nova Scotia ploughing, Tennessee hoeing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Americanism / indigenous sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Grounding in native culture and sympathy with national life enhances popular appeal and moral authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A speaker/author 'surcharged with European learning' but rooted in American life can better move a national audience: trust in, love of, and belief in national life strengthens influence ('thorough Americanism of training and sympathy').

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical influence and moral force
rubrics_metrics.description: Power to condemn without crushing, to denounce yet save from despair; the ability to exert positive control on public opinion by moral and mental vigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure impact by concrete social influence and moral persuasiveness rather than purely aesthetic merit ('He could condemn without crushing...Wherever he went, there went a glance of sleepless vigilance...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Productivity versus literary finish
rubrics_metrics.description: High rate of production and extemporaneous composition often compromises fine literary execution and 'delicate literary ear.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent, hurried output (lecturing, pamphlets) tends to produce loose, diffuse prose or speeches; critics should weigh quantity and timeliness against lasting stylistic quality ('Such a rate of speed is incompatible with the finest literary execution').

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy, concision, and precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to 'hit the mark' with concise force (single bullet) rather than diffuse showers of small shot; value of discriminating, compact expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition and diffuseness are predictable in popular orators; yet higher literary judgment prizes a single telling statement over long-windedness ('Diffuseness is the old Adam of the pulpit...one way with a single bullet, the other with a shower of small shot').

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of rhetorical mode to venue
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetoric shaped by the stage (e.g., Music Hall) tends toward scene-painting, showy masses of effect, and rapidity, often at the expense of finer touches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the rhetorical style fits the audience and venue but also whether it sacrifices permanence for immediate spectacle ('for that great stage his eloquence became...brilliant scene painting...but farewell forever to all finer touches').

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness versus targeted argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendency to cover every point for transient visitors (e.g., Sunday congregation) can broaden appeal but reduce the power of tight, focused argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When many listeners are strangers, a speaker may feel obliged to 'put it all in' — this pleases general audiences but weakens close logic targeted at specialists ('He must put it all in...the people's got the whole latitude and longitude of Theodore Parker').

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of discrimination and subtle insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity for fine discrimination, delicate analysis, and entrance into the sphere of subtle ideas (often contrasted with Emerson's finer sentences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical judgment should note when an author states broad truths but misses subtleties, delicate allusions, or the 'mainsprings of character' in portraiture and criticism ('the delicate mainsprings of character had been missed...subtile beauties puzzle him').

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to changing contexts and nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness of altered phases or finer aspects of movements/current events; avoiding obsolete or misapplied critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether commentary recognizes new forms (example: Parker criticizing revivals as if in older style, missing gentler types of religion). Critics should look for contextual attunement rather than rote opposition ('he did not see that the height of the storm had passed by').

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and risk of self-plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent production across formats (sermon, lecture, speech) leads to the same essential content re-printed under many names, which may indicate over-repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge re-use of material: reworking with new illustrations/statistics can hide repetition, but persistent recycling weakens originality and literary value ('It is astonishing to look over his published sermons...the same stirring speech has been re-printed').

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral steadfastness and truth-telling
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when missing subtleties, a writer/speaker must be judged on whether, seeing truth, he proclaims it and gives it force and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A crucial standard is consistency in moral proclamation and courage: 'it will never discover an instance where, seeing, he failed to proclaim it, or, proclaiming, failed to give it force and power.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity to constituency / national voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Being genuinely representative of a social constituency (e.g., 'poet of the people') and drawing from native traditions and legends strengthens lasting reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the poet/orator's origins and sympathies allow him to authentically voice a group (Whittier as 'Tyrtaeus' of moral agitation and preserver of New England legends). Authenticity can be a distinct, valued function apart from elite literary traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity, directness, and genuineness (poetic style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear, direct, genuine expression often trained by political agitation (e.g., anti-slavery) yields effective moral poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value simplicity and the ability to produce strong effects by common means; activism can refine terseness and moral clarity ('That gave a training in directness, simplicity, genuineness').

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical ear and metrical facility
rubrics_metrics.description: An ear for music (melody and rhythm) is important to poetic effectiveness; lack of musical training or natural ear limits verse to simple strains and ballad metres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate metre and melodic quality: mistakes or lack of confidence about rhythm can cause poets to alter better lines under external criticism. Example: Whittier's substitution and later restoration of a line show sensitivity to musical felicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of local detail and legend
rubrics_metrics.description: Skillful use of place-names, local legend, and vernacular detail enhances poetic authenticity and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local specificity (proper names, vernacular phrasing) creates atmosphere and can be decisive to a poem's success ('The dark pines sing on Ramoth hill...The sweetbriar blooms on Kittery-side').

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint in moralizing and avoiding dilution
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoiding over-obtrusive moralizing and repetitive reiteration of simple morals preserves poetic interest; occasional dilution is a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should note when a poet 'obtrudes his moral a little' or repeats the same simple moral too often; balance didactic purpose with aesthetic restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic correctness versus characterful lapses
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor slips in grammar or pronunciation may be forgiven as whim or oversight, not ignorance, but should be noted as defects when they distract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether quirks (e.g., accenting 'romance' on the first syllable) are harmless character or weaken literary effect; overall literacy matters even when occasional slips occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation by political engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Active participation in political causes (e.g., anti-slavery) shapes poetic voice, producing directness and preventing mere literary detachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how activism informs style and subject matter: such training can be a 'tonic' that yields ethical vigor and a distinct mission, at the expense of purely aesthetic concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longevity judged by quality of sentences and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-term literary reputation depends on stylistic quality — the single golden sentence — rather than popularity or quantity of output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure work by its memorable sentences and stylistic finish (contrast Parker's wide influence vs Emerson's enduring sentences). Quantity/popularity are ephemeral; style determines posterity ('History...judge each author by his most golden sentence').
